The name of Tripura was given to the district in honor of the famous Matha Temple at Odeypoor in Hill Tipperah, which was dedicated to the sun. Mahomed ‘Toghul invaded Tipperah about A. D, 1279, and carricd of much plunder with him; among other things one hundred and sixty elephants. Again about 4. D, 1345, Ijlas Khaja invaded Tippcrah ( 2 ) or Jajnuggur, as it was then called, and plundered it. The Raj of Tipperah preserved its independence up to the time of Shuja-ud-din, who subju- els Review, Decomber pated it in 1733 A. D., and made it a province of the Great Mogul Empire.* Superficially, the country presents a continued flat and open surface, the land consisting of extensive and well cultivated fields, and intersected in all dircc- tions with numerous rivers and khalls, which are partially influenced by the tides. Near the large rivers the lands are under water during the rainy scason. AJ] communications and transport arc effected by means of boats, except during the few months of the hot weather when the village foot-paths are resorted to. The khalls are navigable throughout the year for small boats. Hackeries are almost unknown. Surface of the country. The surfacc,soil in the low lands is light and sandy, but in the higher parts, the country possesses a deep alluvial soil, alternating with bands of clay and sand. The features of

the country on the boundary of Hill Tipperah differ considerably from the champaign. The hills present the appearance of table-land, with an avcrage height of forty feet above the plains, and are covered with forest, in a state of naturc, avd wherever cultivated, which is only in the valleys between the ridges, good crops of ricc are produced. From the yearly flow of water from the high lands into the marshes between the hills, a good supply is procurable at all scasons for irrigation. Tipperah Hills. —The Tipperah Hills seem to offer advantages for cultivation, the soil being decomposed gneiss. In the valleys the soil is productive, and the facility of storing water is turned to good account. Kx- cellent crops of paddy are raiscd. Almost the whole cotton supplicd to the ncighbouring districts is grown on these hills. In many parts the soil consists of a schistose clay, which falls to pieces with little force and has the appearance of sandstone. Large fragments of dicotyledonous wood are often found; as usual they are convertcd into the material in which they are imbedded, but preserve all their original lincaments. They arc laid down horizon- tally, and have never been found in their original vertical position. In sug) instances we cannot suppose the fossil to be on the spot where the living tree grew and died. Cotton. The most remarkable hills are the Lallmaic, a detached or insulated range within British Tipperah, and five miles west of the Civil Station of Comillah; composed of decomposed gneiss, densely wooded, and twenty-one miles in circumference. From North to South, the range extends ten miles. Cotton is the principal production, and cultivated by the

aid of the Kodalce or hand-spade. The plough is used wherever the surface soil or vegetable mould has been washed into the valleys, and exccllent crops of rice are produced. Lallmaie Hills. Considerable traffic appears to be carricd on between the hills of the Rajah of Tippcrah and the plains ; the produce of the former, principally cotton, is Hanic, between the Tipperah ‘bartercd for salt, cloth, and poultry, but the value of the cotton far excceds the amount of these goods: this, coupled with the duties which are exacted by the Tippcrah Rajah, will diminish the cultivation of the cotton, and which, I belicve, has already taken place. Large quantities of building materials, such as timber, bamboos, thatching grass, and rattan are brought down the Goomtee River from tho hills. The Tipperahs seldom remain in one place beyond two seasons; such is their dread of the Tipperah Rajah’s people. ( 3 ) The Tipperahs are fond of ornaments, and wear rings, bracelets, armlets, and earrings, made mostly of brass and shells. “The men are a short sturdy race, the women more squat cven than the men, but strong and lusty. Face broad, check-bones high, eye amall, and the nose short and flat, with wide nostrils,” and strongly marked Malay countenanccs. Rapid encroachments have been madc on this simple people by the inhabitants of the plains, A great many have been weancd from eating beef. They detest the Bengallces. Nine Kooaka. Five Rungaka. Ten Somka. Within the hill territory there arc nine tribes of Kookecs. Towards Chittagong, they arc divided into four tribes, the Chuckmas, Tippcrahs, Recangs, and Susai. To the north the Umroi, Chutlang, Halam, Baipai, and the Kochak Kokces. Kookeo Tnbea. If Europeans were permitted to hold lands in Hill Tipperah and to embark capital on cotton aud tea plantations, this rich and fine tract of country would be much improved. The cotton that is now raised and sent to the market by the hill men, is badly cleaned, and fetches a low price. There is no reason to doubt that the Tipperah Hills adjoining ( 4) British Tipperah, are capable of producing tca and cotton to any extent, if sufficient capital and enterprise were exerted in the undertaking. The produce consists of

rice, safflower, peas, chillies, indigo, and pulses of many kinds, The cultivation of the sugar-cane is pursucd with some success near the village of Doolalpoor. The process of bruising the cane ison a rude plan, and there 1s great room for improvement in the mechanism for extracting and preparing the sugar or goor. Productions of the District. The kinds of crops or produce most profitable and chiefly cultivated, aro Bctlenuts, Rice, Moong Dall, Linseed, Khesaree, and Muskullye. The total area under cultivation is 1,271,061°38 British Acres. This has been ascer- tained from actual survey. The imports are Oil, Tobacco, English piece-goods, Shocs, Umbrellas, Brass and Copper utensils, Tron and Steel, Salt, Indigo, Spices, Building matcrials, and Cotton. Imports. Cheese, Fish-oil, Dried-fish, and Scetulpatee mats are Pap largely exported to Calcutta and the neighbouring districts. The art of curing fish, is not known. ‘The fish sent to market is unwholesome. They are dried without salt, and a large proportion is far advanced in putrescence. ‘The portion of salt which the poor arc able to procure is very small, and the expenses incidental to transport the dried fish, amount to considerably more than the value of the article. Improved means of transport will stimulate production, and the rural population receive in exchange other articles of use. The principal marts for exportation and importation are Comillah, Serael, Brahmun- baree, Chonta, Jaffurgunj, Chandpoor, Ilajeegunj, Chetowsee, and a few others. These are so situated as to cegnmand water carriage. Principal Marts Comillah, the Sudder station and capital of the district, stands on the southern bank of the River Goomtce in Lat. 23° 28’ N., Long. 91° 14’ E., and con- Towns and Villages. : tains

twenty-four Pucka houses. The roads about the station arc very good and well bridged. The chicf trade is in Rice, of which large quantitics are sent to Calcutta for export. The public buildings con- sist of the Circuit house, the Jail, and Public Offices of the Collector and Magistrate. In the Government School there are at present one hundred and nivety-one scholars. ‘The charity Hospital rnd Out-offices cost Rupees 5,715-11-6. The daily average number of prisoners in the Jail is 492, who manufacture divers kinds of articles of good materials, which are sold below the markct rates. The atmospherc is damp, and much infected by malaria rising from stagnant waters. The climate becomes unhealthy immediately after the rains, but the sea brecze which prevails from the south, from April to November, is very grateful to the European constitution, and lowers the tem- perature considerably. Comillah is better known to the Natives as Tripura. Kaleckacho contains 1,425 houses; Scracl five pucka houses and 700 huts; Chonta 500 huts; Talshac one pucka house and 700 huts; Moolgaon 1,111 huts. ( 5 ) In the district there are thirty-nine villages with more than two hundred and fifty houses each, two hundred and thirty-six Iliudoo Temples, and one hundred and fifty Mosques or Mahomedan places of worship. The Native towns and villages are gencrally built in vast plantations of Mangoes, Bamboos, and Palms. Several of the plantations havo run into a wild state, harbouring wild Pigs and Leopards. Sanatory measures are totally neglected. The villages are surrounde!l with low Jungle and rank vegetation. ‘The huts arc mostly thatched with grass ; a few have mud walls and tiled roofs. Brahmunbarce contains a Deputy Magistrate’s

and Moonsiff’s Cutcherry, Thannab, and Post Office. The Police Chowkcy is at Narsirnuggur to the north of the district. The Thannah Stations are Brahmunbarce, Gurecppoora, Thannah in the village of Nobinuggur; Akhanuggur Chowkey in the village of Emamnuggur; Thannahs Kusbah, Thorlah, Davodkandce, Laksham, Juggernath Diggec, Chagulnaya, Hajccgunj, and Nursingpoor. In the villages of Sreemodec, Doolalpoor, Brahmun Chur, Mosimpoor, Bhober Chur, and Akhanuggur, there arc Indigo Factorics conducted by Europcans. The ruins of a factory are to be secn in Shobarampoor. The Megna forms the boundary of the district on the west side and separates it from Mymensing, Dacca, and Backergunge. Opposite to Chandpoor, the Megna rcceives the waters of the Ganges and Brambhapootra, and by the union of these three immense rivers, the channel is considerably cnlarged and studded with numerous islands and sand banks. It continues its course southward, and empties itsclf into the Bay of Bengal. The navigation of this river is attended with various difficulties ; by night it is entirely unsate. Boats are often destroyed by trees floating down. Trees that are fastened by their branches into the bottom of the river, and are only a few inches of the surface, are still more dangerous. The river in its upper part is narrow. In the time of Major Rennell, the confluence of the Megna and Bramhapootra was sixty miles further north, near the village of Bhyrub Bazar, Rivers. The Goomtce comes from the Tipperah IIills and enters the district cight miles cast of Comillah ; after passing the station, it flows to the north of the Lallmaie and Mynamuttee Hills. Its course is through the whole extent of the district from cast to west and falls

into the Megna River at Daoodkandee. The entire length of the Goomtce, including the tortuo- sitics, is sixty-six milcs, and the point where it enters the district from the Tipperah Hills to Daoodkandce where it joins the Megna, is only thirty-six miles. It is navigable for small boats throughout the year, but during the rains the channcl is filled and has a rapidity that is scarcely cofhpatible with navigation upwards. Timbcr and bamboos from the hills are floated down in rafts. The Dakatcca flows through the southern portion of the district and is fed by numerous hill streams. After passing Laksham, Chctowsee, and Hajcegunj in a westerly direction, it sweeps suddenly round to the southward six and a half miles cast of Chandpoor, and empties itself into the Megna, a little above the village of Raipore, in the district of Noacolly. The surface of the country is intersected in all directions with numerous Khalls. The following are the principal ones entering the district from Hill Tipperah:—Khuncajorce at the junction of the Sylhet, Tippcrah and Hill Tippcrah ; Gazarcca, Lahore, Roopa, Howrah, B ( 6 ) fall into the Tectas near the village of Debgram, Sony, Kooree, Scnai, Phootick, Chapatolly, Gurdon, Doolaie, Bakeea, Kalapance, Bejoy, Hloorcemangul, Kakdee, and Pugla. The rivers and khalls iu the district are very tortuous and not sufficiently straight to admit of bcing profitably navigated by country boats. The cheapest mode of conveyance is by rivers, and next by means of canals. A few short canals would be of the greatest utility in inland commerce. The surface of the country having an inclination to the west, an ade- quate supply of water can always be obtained. The

time required by the common country boats to complete their journey from Chetosce village, about twenty milcs east of Hajeegunj, on the southern bank of the Dakateca, to Chandpoor on the Megna, is about seven days. By deepening the Chandpoor Khall from the Dakateea to the Megna, a distance of only six and a half miles, the journey would be shortened by four or five days. The village of Chetosce is the grand medium through which the inland trade in Rice of the districts of Tipperah and Noacolly is carried on. Country sloops and coasting vessels frequently come up to Chand. poor and carry away large cargoes of Rice. Another short canal from Wajcegunj to the Megna River running north-west, may be undertaken with advantage hy deepening the hed of a Khall. The distance from Comillah to Daoodkandee by the Goomtee River can be con- siderably reduced by a few short cuttings. Tho Civil Stations of Comillah and Noacolly can be as easily connected ; the road between them is at present in a wretched condition and not passable for wheeled conveyances, The khalls are not bridged. ‘“No part of Bengal is more capable of improvement than the Eastern Districts. Watered by the best rivers of India, the Ganges, Bramha- pootra, and Megna, and producing a great many articles of consumption and commerce, the resources of these districts can be developed to an ainazing degree.” The only practicable road at all scasons traverses the district from west to cast, or from Daoodkandce to Comillah Icading on to Chittagong, the aggregate length of the road is sixty-three miles; this road is not metalled, but has sixty-one bridges. The secondary roads are

unfitted for whecled conveyances; they are not bridged. Another road branches off from the eastern side of the Mynamuttee Hills to Jaffurgunj on tho River Goomtce ; the bridges on this road are in a most wretched condition. The reads of commu- nication from the Civil Station to the adjacent Thannahs, are simply villago footpaths and much neglected. For the purpose of commerce, there are no roads, and great inconvenience arises during the rainy scason when the country is under watcr. Roads The art by which the products of labor are transferred from place to placc, is csscntial to social advancement, and a pcople, who do not possess it, caunot be said to have emerged from barbarism. In proportion to the perfection of this art will be the cxtent of commerce. Without roads and incapable of communicating with others, a pcople must subsist exclusively upon the productions of its own labor and its own soil. To accomplish in®erchanges of the productions of each particular soil or country, means of transport must be provided. One of the most prominent advantages which attend improved means of transport, is that of lowering the price of all commoditics whatever in the market of consumption and thereby stimulating production. The price paid for an article by its consumer consists of two clements :—1lat, the price paid for the article to its producer at the place of its production ; and 2adly, the expense of conveying it from that place to the consumer. ‘The cost of transport has consequently a great influence upon the price of the products of agricultural labor, If means of transport be provided, the productions find their way casily to the great

centres of population in the towns, and the rural population which produces them, receives in exchange innumcrable articles of use and luxury of which they were before deprived. Good roads have a tendency to stimulate consumption and production and thereby ( 7 ) advance national wealth and prosperity.* No improvement can be expected till a great change for the hetter be mado on the state of the roads. The population consists principally of Mahomedans and ILindoos, with a sprinkling of Tipperahs and Mech, who fled from Muncepoor and were located here by the Rajah of Hill Tipperah. The Lallmaie Hills arc sparingly inhabited by the Tipperahs, who sought refuge within the British territory during the late outbreak of the Kookees. The number of inhabitants in the district, asccrtaincd from actual census is 717,470 souls, contained in 143,342 houses. ‘his gives 4°93 souls to cach house and 270°23 per square mile. Population. Irrigation is not gencrally practised; nor is it necessary. The annual overflow of the rivers and the valuable inundations owing to the heavy periodical rains which begin ®mctimes early in April, and lasts until the end of September, or the middle of October, are of great use in fertilizing the country. Wherever the land is high, and whenever the water is to be raised, the “ Jaut” is used with considerable success. ‘Che “ Jaut” is in the form of a canoe and moves upon a fulcrum placed near its centre. ‘The lever is a long bamboo, one extremity of which is weighted to raise the “ Jaut” when it is filled with water. One man can work a “ Jaut” twelve or fourtecn feet long with facility. On

the eastern side of the district under the Tipperah ITills, the streams are dummecd up, and when a suflicicency of water is collected, it is allowed to flow out into the ficlds. Irrigation. The most valuable manure used is the earth from tanks, dry khalls, and swamps. Ashes are occasionally used, but the Natives secm to be unacquaint- ed with the utility of manure. Wood is so very scarce, that cow-dung is used for fucl. Urine of cattle is well known to be of great valuc as manure, but such is the carclessness of the pcvople that it is allowed to be completely wasted ; large quantities might be easily collected from the ‘ buthdns” or cow-sheds, The land being naturally rich, and the ploughing so very meagre, no impoverishment is observed in the Manures, soll. There are three sorts of pasture lands, 7. e., inundated lands which arc so filled with periodical rains that they never become dry and are overwhelm- cd with weeds; 2d/y, the deserted sites of villages; the pasture here is very good, and during the rainy months, it is the great resource for cattle ; and 3rdly, the sides of tanks and roads, The cows are turned out early in the morning and return in the evening. No care is taken to improve the breed. Pasture Lands The fishcries are conducted in a very rude manner. Theo demand for fish being consider- able, various modes of catching fish are practised. When the lands are inundated during the rainy months, fish is very scarce, and the poor resort to ditches and swamps; the simple method is to raise small banks to confine the water, which is

then thrown out and the fish left dry. The “bund” is very extensively used in small streams, and where the water is shallow, fish caught in this manner are smal!, but in large quantities. ‘The basket trap 1s also much used by the poor who catch fish for their own use. ‘The large “ Besal” nct is used in a boat; the nct is of a triangular form, and is raised and lowered by a lever ; this kind of net is used at all scasons of the yoar, even during the height of the rains when the rivers are flooded, and the largest fish are caught. The largest net used is called the “ Othar,” the diameter of which is sometimes, haat Fisherica, a ee ee ee ee ee ® The Museum of Science and Art, Dionysius Lardner, D.C. L, ( 8 ) sixty fect. The boat is taken to the middle of the stream, the net dropped, and when it sinks to the bottom, the boat is allowed to drift until the sidos of the net are dragged close to cach other when the net is drawn to the shore. The fisheries are let by, the Zcmindars, and each fisherman carns at an average five Rupces cach a month. A district so highly cultivated, the vegetation as might be expected, is not abundant. Timber for building purposes is brought from the Tipperah Hills. Within the district the greater part of the trees grow round deserted villages. The low jungle springing up spontancously, and used as firewood by tho Natives. Vegetable Kingdom. The following is a list of a few of the principal trecs :— Bur (Ficus Indica) commonly

known & the Banyan tree. Grows to a great size and sends down roots which form new stems. ‘The berrics are of a deep red color, leaves large and smooth, color dark green. The Natives consider this tree as the female of the Peepul, and they are supposcd to represent a Brahman and his wife; it is reckoned a gricvous sin to destroy either. Peepul (Ficua It-ligiosa,) this tree is considered holy by the Natives, and has a peculiar elegance from the constant tremulous motion of the leaves, Neem (Melia Azadirachta) another sacred tree. Images are made of its wood. The leaves and oil from the seeds arc uscd medicinally, and in assisting holy men to resist tho allurements of beauty. Kudum (Nauclea Cadumba) wood almost uscless, the fruit is cooked and eaten. Gab (Embryopterix Glutinosa) wood of no value. The fruit is bruised in a mortar, and the juice boiled and miacd with charcoal and applicd to the bottom of boats. Kathbel (Feronia Llephantuin,) the fruit caten by the Natives. The leays have a strong flavour of the anisc. Bel (Cratave Marmelos,) the fruit is caten and used medicinally. Julpai (Lliwocarpur Serratus) known as country olives, though the fruit contains no oil. It is used in currics by the Natives. Seemul (Bombax Neptaphyllum) wood used for building purposes, it is strong and lasts long. ‘The cotton is used for stuffing mattresses and pillows, and has a silky appearance. The stem of the tree is covered with prickles. Flower large and of a deep red color. a Champa (Michelia Champaka) wood of no value. Flowers swect of scent, and by the Natives are offered to the Gods. Jamoon (Calyptranthes Curyophyllifolia)

fruit eaten, wood hard and good for building purposes. Imli (Tumerindus Indica) excellent wood, hard and close graimed, and used for oil aud sugar mills. The fruit is uscd for scasoning food, and the leaves medicinally. Am (Jfangifera Indica) the mangoes of this district are very inferior, and may be con- sidered as the worst in Bengal. The trees producc a great number and of good size, but the (9 ) fruit when allowed to ripen, becomes full of insects. Unripe mangoes are froely used by the Natives in curnes, and pickled with spices in mustard oil. The juice of the ripe mangoe is converted into am-sahut. The wood is very useful, though of an inferior quality, but owing to its being in abundance, it is much used. Kool (Zizyphus Jujuba,) wood close grained, hard and excellent. In this district the tree is small, fruit is not of good quality, and eaten only by the poor. Papaya (Carica Papaya) common fruit, very good. Kamarunga (Averrhoa Carambola) fruit very acid, and not much valucd. Khejur (Phanie Sylvestris) a valuable tree; comes to perfection in five ycars. Tho juice is extracted and made into Goor, which is largely consumed by the Natives, A good tree will yield about (100 Ibs.) one hundred pounds of juice ina month, The leaves are made into mats, Toddy, a sub-acid and intoxicating liquor, is made from the juice. Tal (Boraseus Flabellinformus) used for posts of houses, and a very durable material for building purposes. An intoxicating drink is made from the juice. Leaves uscd for making large fans. Bet (Calamus Rotang) grows spoutancously all over the district. The lcaves resemble the Khejur. The ratans are split

and made into baskets and wicker works and twisted into cables for boats. Betlcenut (Areca Catechu) grows perpendicularly to a height of fifty to eighty feet. Leaves feathery, of a light green color. The nut is largely exported to Rungpore and Dinagepore., Bans (Bambusa Arundinacea) in point of utility, is one of the most important members of the vegetable kingdom. It grows in clumps, and sends up numerous stems, and every year a dozen or morc bamboos are cut. It is usually cultivated. ‘To form a new plantation, a portion of the root with a few stemsis scparated from a clump, and this produces ripe bamboos in six or seven years. Ferns grow luxuriantly in moist and shady places, and are produced by little embryo plants, which arise from various parts of their structure. The principal genera of the Palm tribe are the Date, Betle-nut, Cane, Tal, and Cocoanut. Thcir properties are numerous ; sugar, wine, habitations, flour, oil, cordage, and food, The Sola (Aischynomene Paludos) grows spontancously and in large quantities in swampy lands, It is uscd by fishermen for floating their ucts, and by the Malecs for making artificial flowers. The recds from which the Scetulpntee mats are mado, grow luxuriantly in all the marshes, and aro exposed for sale at the Hauts or markcts. The plants which produce oil, aro the Linseed, ‘Til, and Rayeé or Mustard, but they are raised in small quantities and in the immediate vicinity of villages. The oil-cake of the Linseed 1s used as food for cattle. : ( 10 ) Vegetables cultivated for tho table, occupy a small area, and, with the exception of Chillies, are never exported. Ginger, Turmeric, Fennel,

Coriander, Garlic, and others are carried to the weekly markets and bartered or sold. Chillies are extensively raised, and the consumption is very great. The Chillie fields are ploughed with care, the scedlings which have becn raiscd in the vicinity of villages, are transplanted at a distance of twelvo inches apart ; the plants are carcfully weeded ; when the fruit is gathercd, it is dried in the sim, and putup in gunny bags. The Calcutta market is largely supplicd with Chuillies from this district. Water-melon, Musk-melon, Pineapple, and most of the fruit which the Natives possess, would grow well, but they arc sadly neglectcd and no pains bestowed on ‘their cultivation Paut must be considered as an article of some importance. Of this all tho cordage employed is formed, and is the material of which Country paper is made. The plant is fit for cutting when it is about six feet high. After it has been cut, it is stecped in water and kept down by bamboos. After ten or twelve days, the fibres are so completely scparated that they are taken up by simple washing. The fibres are tied up in bundles, and when dricd are fit for sale. Tobacco, Pawn, and Gunja are cultivated in small quantities, and only sufficient for home use. Indigo and Safflower are the only plants cultivated for producing dycs. Parasi- tical orchids cover the trunks of trecs. The instruments are of the rudest and simplest kind, but well adapted for the wretched breed of cattle and the rich alluvial soil of Bengal. The ploughs arc clumsy in construction and scientific principles are never considered. They are gencrally made entircly of wood, even

Land is held by Zemindars under Lord Cornwallis’ permanent settlement, and by Farmers on temporary leases from Government under Regulation VII. of 1822. The wealthy Zemindars reside out of the district, leaving their Naibs or Gomashtas to collect and remit the rents. A Zemindar usually sublets his lands in Izarahs or Farms, Talooks, Howlahs, and Jotes. The Izaradar holds lands under a terminable lease, and unless restricted by the condi- tions of the scttlement, sublets to Dur-Lzaradars, Jotcdars, and Ryots. Talookdars and How- ladars arc cither permanent or temporary holders of land. If the former, they are termed Kymcc-Talookdars or Kymee-Howladars, but if the latter, Meeady-Talookdars or Mceady- Howladars. Farms are chiefly Government Estatcs, which are let at various leases and rates accord- ing to the condition of the land; some are given free of rent in order to be brought under cultivation. As the leases expire, they are either sold or re-let by the year. In every case of decrement, I’armers can claim a reduction of rent. The following arc the denominations of Tenants subordinate to o TaloBkdar or to a Howladar:—Osut-Talookdar, Neem-Osut-Talookdar, and Jotcdar or Ryot. Necm-Howladar, Osut-Neem-llowladar, Teem-Howladar, and Jotedar or Ryot. The tenants under a Farmer are Dur-Izaradar, Howladar, Neem-Howladar, Osut-Neem- ITowladar, Teem-Howladar, and Jotedar or Ryot. In Estates acquired by Government by purchase for arrears of revenue and leased to a Farmer, the under-tenants enjoy the rights secured during the time of the decennial settle- ment. In such estates, the under-tenants are Talookdars, Howladars, Osut-Talookdars, Osut-Neem-Howlutdars, and Jotedars or Ryots. In all Estates the Jotedar or Ryot is the cultivator of the soil. He pays

his rent to his immediate superior-holder, the latter to the next and so on, till the money reaches the Zemiu- dar, who pays the Government rent. A Zemindar or Farmer, previous to subletting any portion of his estate, causcs a measurement to be made and the land is assesscd at the current rate of the District or Per- gunnah. If the leasc be grantcd in perpetuity, 1 ‘“ Salamec”’ fee of five or ten times the amount of assessment is demanded or half that sum for a temporary settlement. The Naib, Tchsildar, and a host of Peadahs reccive a certain amount. A Zemindar manages his estate through the medium of a Naib or Tchsildar, who resides at the principal Cutcherry, and has a numcrous staff of subordinates, composed of Mohurirs, ( 13 ) Shecah-Nuvees, Chellan-Nuvees, Khazanchce, Potdar, Nazir, Buxce, and Peadahs. The Chellan-Nuvees, Buxee, and Peadahs reccive no fixed salary, but are paid out of the feces levied from the tenants. When the rents are to be collocted, a memorandum called “ Dustuck,” exhibiting the amounts due, is prepared and delivered to the Poadahs who arc authorized to demand and receive the rents. If a tenant is unable to pay, the Peadah demands something in excess of his fee of two annas, returns to the Tehsil Cutcherry and reports tho tenant as absent from the village or unable to attend from illness. It is bounded on the North by the Nipaul Territory, on the South by the rivers Gogra and Ganges, which

form a natural boundary with the districts of Ghazee- poor, Shahabad and Patna, on the East by the district of Tirhoot, and on the West partly by the Gunduck river, which forms a natural boundary, with Raj Bootwul, of the Nipaul Territory, and by the Goruckpoor District. It is divided into two grand divisions, viz., Sircar Sarun and Sircar Chumparun. A SIRCAR CHUMPARUN, IN THE DISTRICT OF SARUN. ahr PRIOT SIRCAR CHUMPARUN. Srrcar Cuumparovn, or the Northern division of the Sarun District, is bounded on the North by the Nipaul Territory, on the South by Sircar Sarun and District Tirhoot, on the East by the Tirhoot District, and on the West partly by Raj Bootwul of Nipaul, with which the main stream of the Gunduck River forms a natural boundary, and by the Goruckpoor District. From Mullye, on the borders of Tirhoot, to a village called Aheera Siswa, on the verge of the great Saul forest in Ramnuggur, the Nipaul frontier is defined by ditches, which are now nearly filled up, except where rivers and streams form a natural boundary, and masonry pillars are erected at irregular distances along the whole of that frontier line, amounting in all to 69, but no figures or marks are cut on them, Some of these pillars have been destroyed by the encroachment of rivers and hill streams, since the Survey in 1845-46, and several of the wooden posts, put up intermediately by the Civil Superintendent in conjunction with the Nipaulese Commissioner during the adjust- ment of the boundary in 1845, have likewise been destroyed. The dilapidated state of the pillars and ditches has already been brought to the notice of the authorities, by the Civil Superintendent; and their repair, I conceive to be of the utmost importance, to pre- vent future litigations. From Mouzah Aheera Siswa, or the laet pillar on the bank of the Goorasin Nuddee, the boundary runs in an almost direct line, through the Saul forest to Bickna Thoree, where a wooden post is put up on the summit of

the Soomaysur range or the Thoree hill, at the foot of which flows the Kodyee Nuddee, and at its junction with the Chituha Nuddee, right below the Nipaulese Thannah, the two streams uniting assume the name of “ Pundyee” River. On this line it was intended to put up fourteen wooden posts, pits had been dug for the purpose, and the posts prepared, but they were never erected ; and several of these posts have since been washed away, or otherwise destroyed. From Bickna Thoree the boundary runs along the high unbroken or continuous range of the Soomaysur hills, overlooking the valley of Mauree and Chitamun of Nipaul, until it reachcs the source of the Puchnud River, from whence the stream of the Puchnud, flowing South and then West to its junction with the Gunduck River at Trebenee, is the boundary between the two States. 2 Sircar Chumparun consists of five Pergunnahs with several Tuppehs or minor sub- divisions, the areas of each of which are detailed in Tabular statements. Sircar Chumparun Contains 2,666 estates or complete villages according to the Civil Superintendent’s list, with a superficial area of 2,420,0782 British statute acres or 3,781°35 square miles. The Government jumma is very light, and the rate of assessment on the total area, including hills and forests, is only 3 annas 9,5, pie per acre. The number of houses, per Police réturns of the Magistrate, amounts to 140,399, and the population to 721,295 Hindoos, 140,162 Moosulmans, or 861,447 souls, giving an average of 6°13 per house, and 227:8 per square mile. But the Magistrate in furnishing this statement of the number of houses and population, expresses his doubts as to its

accuracy ; and considering the great paucity of inhabitants in the North-Western purts of Chumparun, 1 think we would arrive at a nearer approximation to the truth by assuming three individuals per house, which gives a population of 421,197, or an average of 111°38 souls per square mile. The country to the South and East assimilates to the Sarun and Tirhoot Districts, and is an almost entire level. To the North and North-West, it gradually begins tu undu- late, and about Ramnuggur and Tuppeh Rajpoor Sohureea, it assumes a rugged appear- ance, as it advances towards the hills and forests. The lands are low and water close to the surface, and irrigation is not practised. The climate is moist, and particularly humid to the North-West, where pulmonic complaints, the internr#tent and bilious remittent fevers are endemics, and the Goitre or bronchocele is very prevalent throughout Chumparun. The soils are Dorus, Muttyar, Bulsoondur and Bulooa, and to the North, rich clay with several strata of decomposed vegetable matter. The harvests are Bhadooee, Khureef and Rubbee; and the principal crops are paddy of various qualities, wheat, barley, poppy, indigo, urhur, maash, maize, vetches and pease, oil seeds, and a variety of edible roots, The staple are, however, rice, poppy and indigo. Saltpetre is manufactured in large quantities throughout the South and Eastern parts of Chumparun and shipped to Calcutta, and other nearer markets. ‘The principal river is the Gunduck, which nearly skirts this subdivision to the South and South-West, and is navi- gable throughout the year for boata of 1,000 to 1,500 maunds’ tonnage, and traffic is carried on to a great extent by means of this river, for the exports of

rice, ol seeds, opium, indigo, &c. ; and imports of salt, cotton and other goods, from the Eastward. The Gun- duck is, however, a difficult river to navigate, owing to its narrow channel during the cold and hot seasons, and the terrific impetuosity of its current during the rains, when boats can with great difficulty pass up the rapid stream. There are besides the Bagmuttee, the Hurha or Sikrehna which assumes the name of Boor Gunduck or little Gunduck, as it reaches the Tirhoot District, the Lal Bukya, Khujooa, Teeur, Dhunowtee, with numerous tributaries which intersect this division. There are regular ferries at the principal ghats on the high roads leading across the Gunduck, Bagmuttee and little Gunduck Rivers; the other rivers becoming fordable after the rains. The principal roads which pass through Chumparun are from Chupra, Moozufter- poor and Patna, to Moteeharee, Soogowlee and Bettiah; from Bettiah to Goruckpoor vid Buguha; from Bettiah vid Ramnuggur to Trebenee and Nipaul; from Moteeharee to Mullye, and then to Nipaul, and the high road from Soogowlee to Katmandoo ; besides numerous cart roads and bullock tracks which intersect this division. — Bettiah is the capital of Chumparun, where the Maharajah resides, and a Sub- Deputy Opium Agent has recently been stationed; and where there is likewise a Roman Catholic Priest located. Moteeharce is the Civil Station, where a Magistrate 3 and his Deputy, a Sub-Deputy Opium Agent, and a Subordinate Medical Officer are stationed, and there is likewise a Moonsiff’s Kutcherry; Soogowlee is the Military Cantonments of a Corps of Irregular Cavalry. The other places of note are M yheee, Mullye, Halo-Koaree, Shewhur, Ramnuggur, Buguha, Gobindgunj, Kisureea and Tre- benee, where two

fuirs are annually held during the months of “ Phagoon” and “ Cheyte,” where the Nipaulese assemble in large bodies, and the people from Goruckpoor, Azimgurh, Sarun and Chumparun, collect at the fairs to dispose of cloths, brazen vessels, &c., and they purchase knives, iron ores, iron vessels and drugs brought by the Nipaulese. There are several indigo and steam-engine sugar factories in Chumparun, situate chiefly to the East, adjoining Tirhoot, in Pergunnahs Myhsee and Bubra; the principal ones being Bara, Seerah or Seeraha, Pureywa, Rajpoor, Tetureca, Amooa, Jumooawan, Peepra, Toorkwulleea and Moteeharee; besides their outworks. In Chumparun only, 88 villages have been measured by Khusrah, giving an area of 102,831 British acres or 160-67 square miles. The local beegah measure fluctuates from 7% haths to 1! hath luggee, and consists of 5,625, 6,400, 6,944°4, 9,025, 11,025 und 12,100 square yards. PERGUNNAH MYHSEE. Prercunnan’ Myusex is bounded on the North by Pergunnah Semrown, on the South by Pergunnahs Gudehsur and Bisarch, District Tirhoot, on the East by Pergunnah Bubra, and Pergunnahs Moorwah Kulun and Tureeanee, District Tirhoot, on the West by Pergunnah Mujhowa. A detached village formerly of this Pergunnah, named Dureea- poor, being entirely surrounded by the villages of the Tirhoot District, has been i:.eorporated with Pergunnah Moorwah, District Tirhoot, since the introduction of the survey in this Pergunnah, at the recommendation of the Civil Superintendent, and the transfer has been confirmed under Government orders, dated the 13th February 1847, No. 13. The principal rivers are the Bagmuttee and the little Gunduck or Boor Gunduck ; the former skirts the Pergunnah on its Eustern boundary, and the latter part of the way on its Western boundary, and flows in

a South-Easterly direction, partially intersecting this subdivision. These rivers are navigable throughout the year for boats of four and five hundred maunds’ tonnage, but traffic is not carried on to any extent by water carriage. Several ferries are placed on both these rivers, on the high roads, and factory roads. The Khujooa and Bukya Nuddees intersect this subdivision, they are fordable, except during the height of the rains, when small ferries are temporarily placed by the villagers for crossing travellers. There are, moreover, several lakes called by the nutives ‘“ muns,’ being old beds of rivers, which unite with the main streams during the rains and afford excellent fishing. The principal roads are from Chuprah to Mullye eid Shewhur in Pergunnah Bubra; from Moozufferpoor to Motceharee and Soogowlee vid Qusbeh Myhsee, and Bara and Peepra indigo factories; from Qusbeh Myhsee tov Sahebgun) and Kurnowl, besides several excellent roads kept up in good repair by the Planters. This Pergunnah is within the Police jurisdiction of Thannahs Dhaka, Kuleeanpoor and Musowrah; none of these Police Stations are located within this Pergunnah, but there ts an out-post at Qusbeh Myhsee. The villages of note are Qusbeh Myhsee or the town of Myhsee, now nearly in ruins, where a Moonsiff was formerly stationed, and a market is daily held. The villages of Joogwulleea, Asa Chupra-oorf Choorma, Put&hee, Surya Gopal, Kore Pukree and Bhun- 4 dar, where markets are held once and twice a week. The Pureywa indigo and steam-engine sugar factory, and the well known Bara, and Seerah ur Seeraha indigo factories, with their outworks, the Tetureea, Rajpoor and Putdhee indigo factories, are all situate in this Pergunnah. The soila are Dorus, Muttyar, and

Bulooa. The harvest Bhadooee, Khurcef and Rubbee; and principal crops are paddy, mukka, wheat, barley, musoor, sugar-cane, poppy, indigo, potatoes and soothnee, vegetables and tobacco. Irrigation is not practised except in dry seasons, for poppy and vegetables sown near the village sites. This Pergunnah is highly cultivated, and about four-fifths may be assumed as under tillage: there are no large tracks of waste, jungle or grass; but there are extensive mango proves; and it is well populated. ‘The climate is salubrious, but moist, partaking of the temperature of Tirhoot. The beegah in use in this Pergunnah consists of 5,625 square yards. PERGUNNAH BUBRA. Prerounnau Bupra is bounded on the North by the Nipaul Territory, where the boundary line is clearly defined by a ditch and masonry pillars except where the Kutore Nuddee forms a natural boundary between the two States; on the South partly by Per- gunnah Myhsee, and partly by the Tirhoot District, which likewise bounds it on the East, and on the West by Pergunnahs Semrown and Myhsee. The only river worth noticing is the Bagmuttee, which once formed a natural boundary with the Nipaul Territory for a very short distance; but owing to the changes of the river and frequent disputes arising there- from between the Nipaulese and British ryots, the main stream no longer forms the boun- dary, but in concurrence with the Commissioners appointed by the “ Durbar” in the year 1845, a straight line of boundary has been formed by the Civil Superintendent, as described in the map of Bubra from post No. 3 to No. 4 with other leading posts to them, Rumbered 1 to 5, two of which have since been converted

into pucka pillars. The Bagmuttee is navigable throughout the year for small boats of 2 or 300 maunds’ tonnage, aud has ferries af all the ghats along the high and village rouds. It traverses through this subdivision and then turns to its South-Western borders, dividing it from Pergunnah Myhsee. There are besides the Lal Bukya Nuddce which skirts this Pergunnah adjoining Pergunnah Semrown, and several Nullahs and streams, being chiefly old beds of the Bagmuttee, some of which are running streams throughout the year, while others are stagnant except dur- ing the rains. These abound with fish of the finest description, and are rented out by the landholders to fishermen. The principal roads which pass through this Pergunnah are from Qusbeh Myhsce to Katmandoo vid Mullye, from Mullye to Moozufferpoor in the South-Last and to Bhowrwa, in the West, the latter being known as the “ Government boundary road," but is much neglected; besides factory roads, which are kept up in good repair by the Planters. There are moreover several tolerable cart roads which intersect this Pergunnah, and which are much frequented by native dealers in conveying grain, cotton, &c., to the different markets and marts within this subdivision. This Pergunnah is within the Police jurisdiction of Thannah Musowrah, a village of that name situate in Pergunnah Bubra, and there are two out-posts in the villages of Ukhta, and in Mullye. The places of note are Shewhur and Mullye, the former is the resi- dence of the Rajah, who at one tinc held almost exclusive possession of this Pergunnah, and the adjoining ones of Myhsee end Semrown, but he is now comparatively straightened in circumstances, having sold the better portion

of his landed property for the liquidation of 5 heavy debts contracted in carrying on lawsuits: the Rajah is nevertheless much respected by his contemporaries residing in his neighbourhood, and the adjacent districts, and has a sufficient income from the wreck of his domains to keep up a shew of dignity, with a toler- able train of elephants and horses, &c. Mullye, or, better known among the natives as, “ Ha- lokooaree,” is the station of the old Chumparun Light Infantry Battalion, and where the marks of a Military Cantonment are quite fresh,—several of the Officers’ bungalows are still in good condition, while others are falling into decay. The beautifully laid out drives about the late Cantonments, and the appearance of the village and its inhabitants, present a degree of cheerfulness even in the midst of desertion. The climate of Mullye is salubri- ous for Europeans, but it is considered too damp for natives of the Southern and South- Western districts; though judging from the appearance of the residents of Mullye, I should suppose the place to be healthy for all classes of natives. The location of British Troops at Mullye afforded, on the frontier, a safeguard from the depredations of the Nipaulese to the native merchants and dealers, hence it became the grand emporium for every description of grain, cotton and cloths, grain being imported in large quantities, from the Nipaul Terraee, and cotton and cloths exported and sold to the Nipaulese. The other villages of note are Ukhta, M uksoodpoor, Kurureea, Umwa Kulan, and Mudhoohun Juddoo-oorf-Doomree, where markets are held once or twice weekly. The indigo and steam-engine sugar factories of Amooa, or Umooa, Jumooawan, and Bhokhuruha are

situated within this Pergunnah in villages of those names, and there is a saltpetre manu- factory in Mullye, besides a few European resident dealers in grain, seeds, horns, hides, &c. The soils are Dorus, Muttyar and Bulooa; harvests are Bhadooee, Khureef and Rub- bee, and principul crops are paddy, grain, wheat, barley, mussoor, soothnee, vegetables, chillies, tobacco, indigo and poppy. Irrigation is not practised. ‘This Pergunnah is highly cultivated, and about four-fifths of the land is under tillage. It is well populated, and the inhabitants are in a flourishing state, and contented with the low rate of assessment. This Pergunnah likewise assimilates to the Tirhoot climate, and in fact the Planters residing here are known as the North-West Tirhoot Planters. The beegah in use in this Pergunnah consists of 5,625 square yards. PERGUNNAH SEMROWN. PEeRGUNNAH Semrown is bounded on the North by the Nipaul Territory, where the boundary line is defined for the most part by a ditch und masonry pillars, except where the Jumnee Nuddee, and old beds of streams called “ Nassees,” form a natural boundary, and partly where the Southern banks of the ruins of Fort Semrown, separates this subdivision from Nipaul. In this place the boundary line runs between the inner and outer walls or banks now in ruins, and covered with brushwood, but the line of demarcation is perfectly clear and discernible. On the South it is bounded by Pergunnahs Myhsee and Mujhowa, on the East by Pergunnah Bubra, with which the Lall Bukya forms a natural boundary, and on the West by Pergunnah Mujhowa, divided by the Teeur and Boor Gunduck Rivers. The principal rivers are the Lal Bukya, Teeur and Boor Gunduck, which

skirts this Pergunnah; and these are navigable for small boats of 2 and 300 maunds’ tonnage, and there are ferries stationed at the several ghats along the principal roads. There are besides numerous minor streams and Nullahs which intersect this Pergunnah. The high roads passing through this Pergunnah ure from Myhsee to Mullye vid Dhaka Thannah, from Moozufferpoor to Nipaul vid Kotewa-oorf Ghora Suhun on the frontier, where a Police Chowkey is stationed, and from Mullye to Bhowrwa, being the 6 Government boundary road; besides several tolerable cart roads. This Perguunah is within the Police jurisdiction of Thannah Dhaka, stationed in the village of that name. The villages of note are Dhaka, Bijbunee, Dhunookee, Burhurwa and Khundturee, where markets are held twice a week; and there is a steam-engine sugar factory in the village of Meerpoor. The soils are Muttyar, Dorus and Bulooa; harvests are Bhadooee, Khureef and Rubbee ; the principal crops are paddy, wheat, barley, gram, mussoor, poppy, potatoes and vegetables. Irrigation is not practised. The state of cultivation, population and climate are precisely similar to that of Pergunnuh Bubra. The beegah in use in this Pergunnah consists of 5,625 square yards. a ET A REF SS PERGUNNAH MUJHOWA. PergunnaH Musnowa, formerly included the Ramnuggur Illaquah, but for the sake of distinction, and owing to the two divisions having independent proprietors and separate boundaries, the Ramnuggur [llaquah has been termed “ Raj Ramnuggur” in the survey maps and statements, and the Bettiah Rajah’s possessions, including a few other petty proprietors, called “ Pergunnah Mujhowa.” Pergunnah Mujhowa thus constituted, is bounded on the North by the Nipaul Territory, extending from the Teeur Nuddee in the North-East, on the borders

of Pergunnah Semrown, to the Ooriah Nuddee, where it reaches the borders of Raj Ramnuggur. Over this line of country, the frontier is well defined by a ditch and masonry pillars, except where rivulets and streams form a natural boundary ; from the Ooriah Nuddee, Pergunnah Mujhowa proceeds in a North-Western direction along the borders of Raj Ramnuggur, until it reaches the “ Isthan Baloo Thapa” (the rude shrine of a Nipaulese, situate on the brow of the South-Western verge of the Doon Hills) and the Puchnud River, from thence Westward, as far as Trebenee “shat on the Gunduck River, The Puchnud River forms a natural boundary between Pergunnah Mujhowa and the Nipaul Territory. It is bounded on the South by Pergunnahs Kuleean- poor, Kooaree, Seepah, Dungsee and Murhul of Sircar Sarun, and Pergunnah Sidhwa Johenah, District Goruckpoor; on the East by Pergunnahs Myhsee and Semrown, and Pergunnah Gudehsur, District Tirhoot; and on the West by Pergunnah Sidhwa Johenuh and Tilpoorah, District Goruckpoor, and by Raj Bootwul of the Nipaul Territory, with which the Gunduck River forms a natural boundary. This immense Pergunnah of Mujhowa is divided into 25 “Tuppehs” or local subdivisions, as detailed with their respec- tive areas, &c., by survey, in the Tabular Statement. The Gunduck River skirts this Pergunnah on almost the whole of its Southern and North-Western boundary. It is navigable throughout the year for boats of 1,000 to 1,500 maunds’ tonnage, but it is a difficult river to navigate during the dry season, when boats can pass only along the main channel which is narrow and in several places merely wide enough to admit one boat to pass with safety; and during the rains

it becomes a perfect torrent. ‘The numerous Snaigs which abound in this river, oblige the navigators to be very careful in steering and rowing their boats. Accidents are of common occurrence, and destruction of boats and curgo the consequence, by their striking against these hidden clumps, and branches of trees in the river. The larger description of boats are seldom taken up higher than Buguha. There are numerous ferries on this river, but the principal ones are at the well known ghats of Kesureea, Sungrampoor, Gobindgunj, Buryarpoor or Teagrahee ghat ; at Buguha, Bhoal Ghat, and Trebenee, su,erior “ Suckwa” or ‘ Saul” timber, cut from the forests of Rajpoor Sohureea and Ramnuggur, is floated down the Gunduck to IJadjeepoor, 7 Sonepoor and Patna, and large rafts of wood for fuel are brought for sale by this river to the different adjacent stations and towns. The Gunduck is the principal river by which grain of every description, indigo, sugar, oil seeds, &c. &c., are exported from Chumpa- run; and sult, tobacco, coarse rice, cotton, English cloths and chintzea, &c., are imported from the Eastward. The Sikrehna River, which flows under Soogowlee, and assumes the name of Boor Gunduck or little Gunduck, when it approaches the borders of Tirhoot, is likewise naviga- ble part of the way throughout the year, for boats of from 300 to 500 maunds’ tonnage. it takes its source from the foot of the Soomeysur range of hills in Ramnugeur, and is known there and in the Western parts of Pergunnah Mujhowa as the “Hurha River,” but it is not navigable much beyond Soogowlee. There are besides the Teeur, Sumohtee, Dhunowtee, Pundyee, Muneearee, Belowr, Ujwan and Dingree

Nuddees, besides secondary streams which intersect this Pergunnah and become perfect torrents during the rains, but are generally fordable during the dry season ; as likewise numerous Nullahs and Nuddees, and ‘‘ Muns” or lakes, the latter being chiefly old deserted beds of rivers. The principal roads which pass through this Pergunnah are from Chuprah vid Gobind- gunj on the Gunduck to Bettiah, Soogowlee, and Motecharee, from Moozufferpoor vid Myhsee, to Moteeharee, Soogowlee, Bettiah, Buguha and Goruckpoor, from Mullye to Moteeharee and Soogowlece, from Kesureea vid Sungrampoor and Gobindgunj to Bettiah : from Soogowlce to Katmandoo, being the principal road to Nipaul; from Bettiah to Ram- nuggur, and from thence to Trebenee, from Bettiah vid Buguha to Trebenee, the Government boundary road from Maullye, along the frontier to Bhowrwa on the Ooriah Nuddee, and from thence skirting the Ooriah to Aheera Siswa in Ramnuggur to the pass over the Soo- maysur at Bikna Thoree by the bed of the Pundyee River to the Nipaul Terraee ; besides numerous village roads and cart tracks. There are bridges and ferries at the several rivers over which the principal roads pass, the ferries being discontinued on the close of the rains except those on the Gunduck River, The town of Bettiah is the chief place of importance. it is the seat of the Muharajah of Bettiah, the landed proprietor almost exclusively of the whole of Pergunnah Mujhowa. His palace is the finest building at Bettiah, and its lofty, handsome domes and minarets, and his gilded high Shewalah, or Pagoda, built entirely of Chunar stone, situate a short distance to the East of the palace, are visible from a great dis- tance. There is,

moreover, a Roman Catholic Church in the town of Bettiah, and there are many native converts to the Romish creed, who reside in its vicinity on a piece of land, a grant, in perpetuity, to the Catholic Priest, given by the ancestors of the present Maharajah. The village of Choohurree, situate about three miles North of Bettiah, is likewise in farm by the Priest, and the inhabitants are entirely native Christians, some of whom culti- vate the land, but the principal portion of the native Christians are brought up as carters or handy-craftsmen. They excel in the manufacture of straw and bamboo mats, baskets and large and small bamboo ribbed “ chattahs,” covered with colured wax cloth, which meet with ready purchasers at Bettiah, Moozufferpoor, Chuprah and Patna, both for private use, as well as for exportation to Bengal and the North-Western Provinces. A Sub-Deputy Opium Agent has recently been stationed at Bettiah, the Chumparun division being found too extensive for the control of the Officer in that branch of the service. There are several minor native agency houses in Bettiah, and trade is carried on by the native merchants in grain, sugar, cloths, &c. The next places of importance are Moteeharee, the civil station of Chumparun, where a Magistrate and his Deputy, a Sub-Deputy Opium Agent, a Subordinate Medical Officer, and a Moonsiff are stationed ; and Soogowlee, the military station, occupied by a Corps of Irregular Cavalry. The climate of Moteeharee and Soogowlee is considered salubrious, 8 the moisture in the atmosphere being very agreeable to the European constitution. The water, however, is inferior, and of a tendency to excite the glands of the neck, and cause Goitre

or bronchocele, a very prevalent complaint throughout Chumparun. The villages of note are Buguha, Gobindgunj, Sungrampoor and Kesureea on the Gunduck River, where there are large bazaars, and markets are held twice a week; and Rutwul in Tuppeh Manpoor, Chowdund, Jugdeespoor in Tuppeh Khudda, Dhekuha and Soorujpoor, in Tuppeh Mudwul, Sukhwa Khas, Muchurgawan in Tuppeh Putjirwa, Loheeyar in Tuppch Soogaon, Nurkuteea in Tuppeh Buhas, Singarpoor in Tuppeh Gepala. Koondowlee in Tuppeh Gondowlee, Urrey-Raj in Tuppeh Hurna Tand, where there is a high Shewalah, and a fair is annually held in the month of “ Phagoon.” Lowreea Bazaar, in Tuppeh Bulooa, where there is a “ Zowr” or stone pillar, with a carved lion’s head on ita surface, and well known as one of “ Bheem Seyn’s Lathees.” In this village of Lowreea 18 to be scen, on the banks of the Sikrehna River, the ruins of an ancient fort called “ Now- nidh Gurh,” which is visible from a great distance, and has the appenrance of low hills. There are nine mud embankments, running North and South, and seven running East and West, with marks of brick and mud bastions ; these are overgrown with thick high jun- gle. The villages of Seeta Koond and Bedee-bun in Tuppeh Mando, likewise deserve notice on account of the deep veneration with which the Hindoos visit the celebrated excavated tank, and a pukka reservoir and Shewalahs situated within a short distance of each other. It is said to be the place of the nuptial of “Ram Chunder,” the 7th Mythological Hindoo incarnation, and the conqueror of “ Lanka” with “ Seeta,” the daughter of Rajah Junuk of Junukpoor, in the Nipaul Terraee. In

all the villages above noted, there arc bazaars, anc markets are held once or twice a week. In Tuppeh Rajpoor Sohureea, on the borders of the Saul forest, is to be seen the ruins of the “ Bawun Gurhec,” or ancient remains of 52 forts. This place is well worth the researches of the antiquarian. It is said to have been the residence of Rajah “ Burrahk,” who is supposed to have been contemporary with the Rajahs of Semrown Gurh and Nownidh Gurh, of Lowreea Bazaar. From the appearance of the country, and the immense forest round the “ Bawun Gurhee,” wg would suppose that Rajah Burrah must have built his fortress in the wilds of Rajpoor Sohurcea, as o retreat for himself and his followers from the invasions or depredations of his more powerful neighbours of Semrown and Lowreca to the South-East, and the hill tribes of Nipaul and Bootwul to the North and North-West. The remains of mud walls or embankments, and traces of brick walls here and there, are to be clearly scen. There are several tanks and pukka wells within these walls, which clearly denote that this place, now surrounded by thick forest, was once inhabited by a large body of men. In addition to the sudder Thannah at Moteeharee, there are Police Thannnahs at Bettiah, Buguha, Kuleeanpoor, and Gobindguny; and Police Chowkies are stationed at Jugdeespoor in Tuppeh Khudda, at Rutwul in Tuppeh Manpoor Chowdund, at Deeboo- gunj, Ruksowl, and Soogowlee in Tuppeh Soogaon, at Kesureea in Tuppch Dowlutta, and at Toleh Kookoorbhooka. The following indigo factories are situated in this Pergunnah, viz., Peepra indigo factory in Tuppeh Belwa, with its outwork in Dynce Muth

in Tuppeh Belwa ; Tookwalleea indigo factory in Tuppeh Mudhwul; Moteeharee indigo and steain- engine sugar factory in Tuppeh Mudhwul; Burhurwa and Poochureea indigo factories in Tuppeh Dowlutta, being outworks of the Moteeharee concern; Soogaon indigo factory to the South of Soogowlee ; and Choruhee indigo factory i Mowzah Buldeeha of Tuppch Manpoor Chowdund, which has been shut up for some years. There are besides two bungalows and sugar godowns now in ruins near Buguha. Soils are Dorus, Muttyar, Bulsoondur and Bulooa; and harvests are Bhadooee, Khureef and Rubbee. Principal crops are paddy, kodou, joar, maash, tecl, koorthee, barley, wheat, 9 gram, sugar-cane, poppy, indigo, mussoor, potatoes, roots, kc. Irrigation is not practised. The Eastern portion of this Pergunnah, adjoining Pergunnahs Myhsee and Semrown, is the most productive and well populated. A line might be drawn from the junction of Goruckpoor, Sarun and Chumparun, to Bettinh, and from thence to the trijunction of Ramnuggur, Mujhowa, and Nipaul on the Ooriah Nuddee. To the East of this line the country partakes of the soil und climate of Myhsee and Tirhoot, where indigo and poppy ure grown in great abundance, and the soif'is rich and eapable of producing almost every description of crops. There are small tracts of low jungle here and there, along the banks of rivulets and streams, except in Tuppeh Dooho Sooho, where there are larger tracts of low jungle adjoining the Nipaul Territory, and plots of high grass jungle are to be seen interspersed throughout these minor subdivisions of Mujhowa. The country to the West and North-West of Bettiah is not so well cultivated, nor so populous, as the Eastern parts of Mujhowa; and in Tuppehs Chigwan Butsura

and Manpoor Chowdund, about one-third of the land is waste and unproductive. The Northern portion adjoining Ray Ramnugyur is chiefly covered with high grass, which is cut and conveyed to Bettiah, Soogowlee, &c., for thatching, and otherwise appropriated for grazing cattle; and the Southern parts of these Tuppehs, on the right bank of the Gunduck River, are chiefly waste, being covered with large patches of “ Jhow” and reed jungle, and the mimosa catechu, from which large quantities of catechu is made and aold at Bettiah, Goruckpoor, Patna, &c. The central portion of these two Tuppehs, ubout Buguha however, is under a high state of cultivation, and is densely populated. In these parts, sugar-cane is grown in great ubundance, and may be considered the staple production of this part of the country. The soil of these two Tuppehs are peculiar, the Southern portion of the country partakes of sand and slight coatings of clay, brought on by the inundations of the Gunduck, the central portion is a rich Dorus or admixture of mould and sand, and the Northern part consists of Bulsoondur and Bulooa. Tuppeh Rajpoor Sohureea partakes of the Ramnuggur soil and climate. It is very thinly populated, and in scattered portions, by the “ Tharoo” Raee, and about one-fourth of the area may be assumed as under tillage; one-fourth being waste, and grass; and about half its area covered with thick Saul forest. The country West and North-West of Bettiah is insalubrious, the intermittent fever in its worst form, being the endemic complaint, which commits fearful ravages amongst the inhabitants, on the breaking up of the rains, and the early part of the cold season. In Pergunnah Mujhowa

is to be seen along the borders of Tuppehs Buhas and Bulthur, a large swamp, called “ Bhds” by the natives, a regular bog where, during the yreater portion of the year, that part of the country is impassable by human beings, as well as by animals. Yet this land produces superior rice, the seed being thrown in the mire by means of canoes, and the crop cut during the cold season by the villagers on canoes, which are propelled by paddles or light oars. This tract of country becomes hardened during the hot season, when water oozes out of the surface and runs off into neighbouring streams, and at that time, travellers can walk over the better portion of the swamp with safety, taking the precaution however of feeling their way by means of sticks and baumboos as they advance, from fear of suddenly coming upon unsafe ground and being swallowed up in the bog. This Pergunnah of Muyhowa at the time of the perpetual settlement was chiefly waste; the Northern parts were covered with forest which are now inhabited, and under beautiful cultivation. There is a great paucity of inhabitants in the North and North-Western parts, and the rate of asseasment between the zemindar and cultivator is low, when compared with the neighbouring Pergunnahs. 10 The beegahs in this Pergunnah consist of 5,625, 6,400, 6,944.4, 9,025, 11,025 and 12,100 square yards. RAJ RAMNUGGUR. Ras Ramnveeur is bounded on the North by the Nipaul Territory, the high Soomay- sur range of hills being the acknowledged line of demarcation between the two States, on the South, and South-West by Pergunnah Mujhowa, on the East by the Nipaul Territory, with which

the old bed of the Ooriah Nuddee forms a natural boundary up to Aheera Siswa, on the borders of the great Saul forest, along which line, or on the right bank of the Ooriah Nuddee, several pukka masonry pillars exist; and from Ahcera Siswa to Bickna Thoree where a wooden post was put up on the Soomaysur range of hills by the boundary Commissioners in 1845,—the boundary runs in a straight line. Fourteen pits had been dug along this line for the erection of wooden posts, to serve as landmarks between the two States; but unfortunately these posts were never put up, and several of them which were laying on the ground at the time of survey in 1845-46, have since been washed away, or otherwise destroyed; the boundary line however can always be easily ascertained hy simply burning the grass, which grows up annually along the cut tine. On the North-West, the Puchnud River forms a natural boundary with Nipaul, (i. e.,) from the sonrce of the Puchnud, to Chuoreea Tuleh below the “ Isthan Baboo Thapa.” This Raj or Thalooka is subdivided into three Tuppehs, viz., Ramgeer, Jumhowlec and Chigwan, including the Doon valley. The Southern portion of Ramgeer is tolerably salubrious and is pretty fairly cultivated and populated. Tuppeh Jumhowlee is the next, and Chigwan or the Western subdivision is both unhealthy, and is very scanty in its inhabitants, and poorly cultivated. In Ram- geer one-tenth of the area may be reckoned under the head of forest hills and low jupgle ; in Jumhowlee about half and half, and in Chigwan one-third of the area by survey cau alone be classed under the head of cultivated and

culturable ; one-third being forest and hills, and one-third waste, high grass and brushwood. The climate of Raj Ramnuggur is notorious for its insalubrity, the intermittent and bilious remittent fevers of the worst type being endemics in these places. The only times of the year thut a person can proceed into these wilds, are the months of January, February and early part of March, The “ Owl,” or jungly fever, assuming the very worst type of the typhus, is very prevalent during the hot and rainy months, except to the aborigines of the forest, who have become acch- mated, like the “ Oveleeas,” who traverse the road through the Nipaul Terraee, at all times and seasons, The fort of Soomaysur, however, now in ruins, and the open table land about it, would make an excellent sanitarium, the height of the fort above the lowland being above the reach of malaria. A good road oyer the present difficult pass might easily be made with some expense, from Goburdhunna and Jaree Pance, and a dik communication established from Soogowlee to the fort vid Bettiah and Ramnuggur. The principal river in Raj Ramnuggur is the Hurha, which takes its rise from the Soomaysur range North of Mouzah Gurdee in the Doon, and assumes the name of Sikrehna in Pergunnah Mujhowa, and of Boor Gunduck, or little Gunduck, as it reaches the Tirhoot District. This river is not navigable however up in these parts, and the numerous minor rivers and streams which are tributaries to it, render the “ Hlurha” a perfect torrent during Il the rains, but in the dry season it is generally fordable. The next river to the Hurha is the

Pundyee which takes that name at Bikna Thoree, at the junction of the two hull streams, viz., Chituha and Koodyee, these two take their source in the Nipaul Territory and divide the Soomaysur range at Bikna Thoree. There is an easy and excellent pass at this place into “ Deo-ghat” of Nipaul, and by this route the British Army passed over the Soomaysur range and encountered the Nipaulese during the Goorkha war in 1814-15, A Nipaulese Thannuah is stationed at the junctiof of these two streams near Bickna Thoree. There are moreover the Dorum, Doongyee, Musan Dingrce, Kapun, Bulooee or Dhar and Uchooee, besides numerous rivulets and streams which intersect Raj Ram- nuggur. Gold dust is collected in the Puchnud, Hurha, Bulooce or Dhar, Uchooee and Kapun Rivers during the commencement and termination of the rains, just above the low range, and below the second and third ranges of the Soomaysur hills. ‘The high or boun- dary range being a complete barrier to any water flowing to its South, it is evident that the gold dust 1s washed by the rivers, out of the second or third ridges, within the British Terri- tories, and from the peculiar formation of these hills, which here become more rugged and fearfully precipitous, with light and scattered jungle about them, J um led to conclude that veins of gold may be discovered within these hills, which would amply compensate the Government, for deputing a Geologist and Mineralogist to carry on his researches through this very interesting part of Chumparun, viz., the Doon valley. It is alleged that several thousands of rupees worth of gold dust used to be collected during the reign of the

former Rajah of Ramnuggur: the amount now realized by the Government farmer is very considerably below what is above stated, but this is supposed to arise from the paucity of the tribe who wash for gold, several families of them who for- merly resided in these wilds, and made « regular trade of washing for gold dust, having deserted from over-taxution. The inhabitants are chiefly “ Zharovs,” a wild race, evidently descendants of Tartars who inhabit the Northern parts of Ramnuggur. To the South and South-East however, there are a few villages inhabited by country tribes of Hindoos and Mahommedans. The “ Tharoos” pay but a slight revenue in proportion to the extent of their cultivation; but they are un honest sort of people, and are proverbial in the regularity of their payments of the Government “ Kists.” The belt of forest to the North of Ram- nuggur contains very valuable timber,—the Saul or Sukhwa timber, of superior quality and lengthgis found in these parts, and annually felled and exported by the Gunduck River, to Hadjeepoor, Patna and other towns and stations. The high grass jungle is seen in extensive plots, covering hundreds of acres of land. This grass is used for thatching, and all the grass to the Southward is generally sold for 3 annas to 4 annas per cart load; the purchasers meeting the expense and trouble of cutting, but the greater portion of the high erags (owing to the difficulty of procuring carriage and the great distance from any city or place of note) is burnt annually by herdsmen, to admit of the new shoots springing up for grazing of cattle. Bullocks, cows and buffaloes go im

extensive herds to Ramnuggur from the plains of Sarun and Chumparun, and from the Eastern parts of the Goruckpoor district. The charge of 3 annas per head for bullocks, 4 annas for buffaloes, and 5 rupees per 100 cows, is levied per scasun, which the herdsmen pay readily for the beautitul and nourish- ing pasturage which Ramnuggur affords. The whole of Raj Ramnuggur is under the Police jurisdiction named “ Thannah Bunjurcea,” and lately stationed at the village of Burbecro, Tuppeh Deoraj, Pergunnah Mujhowa, the climate of Bunjureea being found highly insalubrious and a number of casualties having occurred there among the Police Officers, There is, moreover, a Police Chowkee at Ramnuggur Adas. 12 The chief village of importance is Ramnuggur, which is the residence of the Rajah of this subdivision; the climate of which is notorious for insalubrity and the inhabitants have deserted to about one-fourth of what they were years ago. The Rajah’s dwelling- house is the only pukka place at Ramnuggur, but is now almost in ruins, owing to the distress and difficulties which the two collateral branches of the family have brought on themselves by lawsuits in the Civil Courts, and the “ Illaquah,” being under the Court of Wards. ‘There is a tolerable bazaar at Ramnuggur, and a market is daily held. There are moreover the villages of Myna Tand, Sendooreea, Bhusooraree, (where Mr. Yule, the Government farmer of Ramnuggur, resides) Singarpoor, Balaspoor and Byreea Kulan, which are well populated for these wilds. They have no bazaars nor markets held in them, and the inhabitants of these parts resort to the markets held at Bhowrwa, Lowreea Bazaar, Mutheea and Hurna Tand, in Pergunnah Mujhowa, for

supplying themselves with such articles as they may require. The principal roads are from Bettiah vid Bhowrwa and Aheera Siswa along the Ooriah Nuddee, by the “ Bikna Thoree” Pass, over the Soomuaysur range into Deo- what and the Nipaul Territory, from Bhusooraree to Ramnuggur, Bettiah to Ramnuggur vid |.owreea Bazaar, Ramnuggur to Nipaul vid Mahajogin, and pass over the Soomaysur range, and Ramnuggur to Trebenee. ‘There is likewise a good cart road from Aheera Siswa to Gurdee in the Doon, besides much frequented footpaths and passes over the Soomaysur, at fort Soomaysur, the Ilurha, and the Kapun Rivers. Soils are Muttyar, Dorus and Bulooa, and in the Doon valley and foot of the hills, a rich mould with several strata of fine decomposed vegetable matter. Harvests are Bhu- dooee, Khureef and Rubbee; and the principal crops are paddy of various qualities and descriptions, barley, peas, oil seeds, mussoor and a little urhur and tobacco. ‘The pro- ductions gradually decrease in quantity and quality. From the South-Eastern borders of Raj Ramnuggur, to the North and North-West, great difficulty is experienced in preserv- ing the crops from wild animals, numerous herds of wild elephants coming in during the rains, and early in the cold season, to eat up the paddy cultivation, and the deer proving very destructive to the Rubbee crops,—elephants are decoyed in the woods of Ramnufgur by means of rope loops and nooses put round py trained elephants, but very few of these sayacious animals have been captured within the last few years. Irrigation is never practised; and there are few pukka wells to be seen throughout this subdivigion, water being plentiful from the numerous streams and watercourses which

abound. The beegah in use in this subdivision consists of 11,025 square yards. The soil of Ray Ramnuggur is very rich and productive, but owing to the unheal- thiness of the climate and the consequent paucity of inhabitants, joined to the depreda- tions committed by wild animals on the crops, the Northern portions of Ramnuggur, and especially the Doon valley, are but partially cultivated, and very thinly inhabited.
